title: How the Web Works
description: Follow a request from URL to pixels: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, cookies, CORS, caching, REST and the browser rendering pipeline.

chapters.title: URLs, DNS and the Journey of a Request
chapters.summary: What happens between typing a URL and the first byte arriving: URL parsing, DNS resolution and the TCP/TLS connection.

lesson.heading: Anatomy of a URL
lesson.body:
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) tells the browser what to fetch and how. The generic syntax is defined in RFC 3986:

`scheme://userinfo@host:port/path?query#fragment`

- **scheme**: the protocol, such as `https`, `http`, `ws`, `mailto` or `file`.
- **host**: a domain name (`api.example.com`) or an IP literal (`[2001:db8::1]` for IPv6).
- **port**: optional. Defaults come from the scheme: 80 for `http`, 443 for `https`.
- **path**: identifies the resource on the server, such as `/users/42`.
- **query**: key/value pairs after `?`, such as `?page=2&sort=name`. The server receives it.
- **fragment**: everything after `#`. The browser uses it to scroll to an element or for client-side routing. **It is never sent to the server.**

Characters outside the allowed set are percent-encoded: a space becomes `%20`, `&` inside a value becomes `%26`. In JavaScript, use `encodeURIComponent` for a single query value and `encodeURI` for a whole URL (it leaves `/ ? & #` alone). The `URL` and `URLSearchParams` APIs handle encoding for you and are the safest choice.

code.source:
const url = new URL("https://shop.example.com:8443/search?q=red shoes#results");
url.protocol;            // "https:"
url.hostname;            // "shop.example.com"
url.port;                // "8443"
url.pathname;            // "/search"
url.searchParams.get("q"); // "red shoes"
url.hash;                // "#results" (never sent to the server)

url.searchParams.set("q", "a&b");
url.search;              // "?q=a%26b" - encoded for you

lesson.heading: DNS: turning names into addresses
lesson.body:
Computers connect to IP addresses, not names. The Domain Name System (DNS) is a distributed, hierarchical database that maps names to records.

When the browser needs `www.example.com` it checks, in order: its own DNS cache, the operating system cache (and the hosts file), then asks a **recursive resolver** (usually run by the ISP, the company network, or a public service such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8). If the resolver has no cached answer it walks the hierarchy:

- It asks a **root server**, which refers it to the servers for the `.com` top-level domain (TLD).
- It asks the **TLD servers**, which refer it to the **authoritative name servers** for `example.com`.
- It asks the authoritative server, which returns the actual record.

Every answer carries a **TTL** (time to live, in seconds). Resolvers and browsers cache the answer for that long, which is why DNS changes "propagate" slowly: old answers live until their TTL expires. Lower the TTL a day before a planned migration.

Classic DNS uses UDP port 53 (falling back to TCP for large responses). DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt queries so networks cannot read or tamper with them.

lesson.heading: Common DNS record types
lesson.body:
- **A**: name to IPv4 address.
- **AAAA**: name to IPv6 address.
- **CNAME**: alias from one name to another name (`www.example.com` to `example.cdn.net`). A CNAME cannot coexist with other records on the same name, so it is not allowed at the zone apex (`example.com` itself). DNS providers offer ALIAS/ANAME or "CNAME flattening" to work around this.
- **MX**: mail servers for the domain, with priorities.
- **TXT**: free text, used for domain verification, SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
- **NS**: which name servers are authoritative for a zone.
- **CAA**: which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain.
- **HTTPS / SVCB**: newer records that advertise connection hints, such as supported ALPN protocols (`h3`), so a browser can use HTTP/3 on its first connection.

Load balancing and CDNs use DNS heavily: an authoritative server can return different IPs depending on the client location (GeoDNS) or health checks.

code.source:
$ dig www.example.com A +noall +answer
www.example.com.   300   IN   A   93.184.215.14
;; name               TTL  class type value

$ dig example.com MX +short
10 mail1.example.com.
20 mail2.example.com.

lesson.heading: Opening the connection
lesson.body:
With an IP address in hand the browser opens a transport connection:

- **TCP handshake** (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2): SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. This costs one round trip (RTT) before any data flows.
- **TLS handshake** for HTTPS: with TLS 1.3 this adds one more round trip. The client sends the server name (SNI) and the protocols it supports (ALPN, for example `h2` and `http/1.1`).
- **QUIC** (HTTP/3): runs on UDP and combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into a single round trip, or zero for resumed connections.

Round trips dominate latency on mobile networks. A user 150 ms away from the server pays roughly 150 ms for DNS (if uncached), 150 ms for TCP, 150 ms for TLS and 150 ms for the first request before seeing any HTML. This is why CDNs (servers close to users), connection reuse, `<link rel="preconnect">` and HTTP/3 matter.

lesson.heading: The full journey, end to end
lesson.body:
The classic interview question "what happens when you type a URL and press Enter?" ties everything together:

- The browser parses the input: is it a URL or a search term? It may upgrade `http` to `https` if the site is on the HSTS preload list or the browser defaults to HTTPS-first.
- It checks the HTTP cache. A fresh cached response can be used with no network at all.
- DNS resolution turns the host into an IP address (or reuses a cached answer).
- It opens a TCP + TLS connection (or QUIC), or reuses an existing one to the same origin.
- It sends an HTTP request: method, path, headers (`Host`, `Accept`, `Cookie`, `User-Agent` and so on).
- The server (often via a CDN, load balancer and reverse proxy) produces a response with a status code, headers and body.
- The browser streams the HTML into the parser, discovers CSS, JS, images and fonts, fetches them, builds the DOM and CSSOM, runs scripts, lays out the page, paints and composites it to the screen.

You do not need every detail in an interview, but you should be able to go deep on any one step when asked.

keyPoints: A URL is scheme, host, optional port, path, query and fragment; the fragment never reaches the server.
Use the URL and URLSearchParams APIs (or encodeURIComponent for single values) instead of hand-building query strings.
DNS resolution goes browser cache, OS cache, recursive resolver, then root, TLD and authoritative servers.
TTL controls how long DNS answers are cached; lower it before planned changes.
A records map to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME aliases one name to another and is not allowed at the zone apex.
Each new connection costs round trips (TCP, TLS); CDNs, connection reuse and HTTP/3 cut that latency.

questions.prompt: Which part of this URL is NOT sent to the server in the HTTP request?
options: The host `example.com` (sent in the Host header)
questions.explanation: The fragment is handled entirely by the browser (scrolling, client-side routing). The path and query form the request target, and the host travels in the `Host` header (or `:authority` in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3).

questions.prompt: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: URLSearchParams percent-encodes values, so the `&` inside the value becomes `%26` and cannot be confused with a parameter separator.

questions.prompt: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: AAAA (quad-A) records hold 128-bit IPv6 addresses. A records hold IPv4 addresses, CNAME aliases names, and PTR does reverse lookups from IP to name.

questions.prompt: You changed an A record, but some users still reach the old server an hour later. The record's TTL was 86400. What is the most likely reason?
options: DNS changes need a server restart
Resolvers cached the old answer for up to 24 hours
The authoritative server is still serving the old value
questions.explanation: A TTL of 86400 seconds lets resolvers and clients cache the old answer for up to a day. The fix for future changes is to lower the TTL well before the migration.

questions.prompt: Why can't you put a CNAME record on the bare domain `example.com`?
options: CNAMEs only work for subdomains of www
A CNAME cannot coexist with other records, and the apex must have SOA and NS records
Browsers refuse to follow CNAMEs at the apex
CNAMEs only work over DNS over HTTPS
questions.explanation: The DNS specification forbids a CNAME alongside other data for the same name. The zone apex always has SOA and NS records, so a CNAME there would conflict. Providers solve this with ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME flattening.

questions.prompt: On a fresh HTTPS connection over TCP with TLS 1.3, how many round trips happen before the client can send its HTTP request?
questions.explanation: One round trip for the TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and one for the TLS 1.3 handshake. The request can then go out. QUIC merges these into a single round trip.

questions.prompt: `encodeURI("https://a.com/?q=x&y=1")` will encode the `&` and `?` characters.
questions.explanation: `encodeURI` is meant for whole URLs and leaves reserved characters such as `? & / #` intact. `encodeURIComponent` encodes them, which is why it is used for individual values.

questions.prompt: A recursive resolver contacts the root servers for every single lookup it performs.
questions.explanation: Resolvers cache answers, including referrals to TLD servers, for their TTL. Root servers are only consulted when the cached data has expired, which is rare for popular TLDs.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which techniques reduce connection setup latency for a page?
options: Serving content from a CDN edge near the user
Raising DNS TTLs from 60 to 3600 seconds for stable records
Opening a brand new TCP connection for each request
questions.explanation: A CDN shortens every round trip, preconnect performs DNS, TCP and TLS early, and longer TTLs mean more cache hits for DNS. Opening new connections per request adds handshakes, which is the opposite.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the DNS server that holds the definitive records for a zone is called the ___ name server.
questions.explanation: Authoritative servers are the source of truth for a zone. Recursive resolvers query them and cache the results.

questions.prompt: What happens when you type https://www.example.com into the browser and press Enter?
questions.answer:
A strong answer walks the layers and is ready to go deep on any of them:
- The browser decides it is a URL, applies HSTS / HTTPS-first upgrades and checks its HTTP cache (and service worker, if registered).
- DNS: browser cache, OS cache, then the recursive resolver, which may walk root, TLD and authoritative servers. Result is cached per TTL.
- Connection: TCP handshake plus TLS 1.3 (SNI, ALPN to pick h2), certificate validation against trusted CAs; or QUIC for HTTP/3. Existing connections are reused when possible.
- Request: GET / with Host, Accept, cookies and other headers. The response may come from a CDN edge, load balancer and app server.
- Rendering: HTML streams into the parser, which builds the DOM; CSS builds the CSSOM; scripts may block parsing unless async/defer; the browser builds the render tree, runs layout, paints and composites layers to the screen.
- After load, further requests (images, fonts, API calls) reuse the connection.

questions.prompt: Explain how DNS resolution works and where caching happens.
questions.answer:
- The stub resolver in the OS asks a recursive resolver (ISP, corporate, or public like 1.1.1.1).
- The recursive resolver walks the hierarchy if needed: root servers refer it to the TLD servers, TLD servers refer it to the authoritative servers for the domain, which return the record.
- Caching happens at every level: the browser, the OS, the recursive resolver (including the NS referrals). Each answer has a TTL that bounds the cache lifetime.
- Implication: low TTLs give fast failover but more queries; high TTLs give speed but slow changes. Before a migration you lower the TTL ahead of time.
- Bonus points: DoH/DoT for privacy, GeoDNS and DNS-based load balancing, and that negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are also cached.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a CNAME and an A record, and when would you use each?
questions.answer:
- An A record maps a name directly to an IPv4 address (AAAA for IPv6). Use it when you control a stable IP, such as a static load balancer address.
- A CNAME maps a name to another name, and the resolver then resolves that target. Use it to point a subdomain at a provider-managed hostname (a CDN, Heroku, a SaaS) whose IPs change without you knowing.
- A CNAME costs an extra lookup step and cannot coexist with other records on the same name, so it cannot be used at the zone apex; providers offer ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME flattening for that case.
- MX and NS records must not point at a CNAME either.

questions.prompt: Why does latency (round trips) often matter more than bandwidth for page load time, and what can you do about it?
questions.answer:
- Most web resources are small, so the time is dominated by waiting for round trips, not transferring bytes. TCP slow start also limits how much data the first round trips can carry.
- A cold HTTPS load pays DNS, TCP, TLS and the request itself, each costing at least one RTT; on a 150 ms mobile link that is over half a second before the first byte.
- Mitigations: CDNs to move content closer, connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing), HTTP/3 and TLS 1.3 to cut handshakes (0-RTT resumption), preconnect and dns-prefetch hints, fewer origins, caching so that requests are not made at all, and 103 Early Hints to start fetching critical resources while the server thinks.

chapters.title: HTTP Basics: Requests, Responses, Methods and Status Codes
chapters.summary: The structure of HTTP messages, what each method means, and how to choose and read status codes.

lesson.heading: HTTP is a request/response protocol
lesson.body:
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is how browsers, apps and servers exchange data. A client sends a **request**, the server sends back a **response**. HTTP is **stateless**: each request carries everything the server needs, and the server does not remember previous requests unless you add state on top (cookies, tokens, sessions).

The semantics (methods, status codes, headers) are defined once in RFC 9110 and are the same across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Only the wire format changes: HTTP/1.1 is text, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are binary framed. Developer tools show all three in the same request/response form.

code.source:
GET /api/users/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 48
Cache-Control: private, max-age=60

{"id":42,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com"}

lesson.heading: Methods and their guarantees
lesson.body:
Each method has defined semantics. Two properties matter in interviews:

- **Safe**: the request is read-only from the client point of view. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are safe. Crawlers and prefetchers may call safe methods freely, so never change data on GET.
- **Idempotent**: sending the same request N times has the same effect on the server as sending it once. All safe methods plus PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST is not. PATCH is not guaranteed to be.

What the methods mean:
- **GET**: retrieve a representation. No body by convention.
- **HEAD**: like GET but only headers; useful to check size or existence.
- **POST**: process the enclosed data, usually creating a subordinate resource or triggering an action.
- **PUT**: create or fully replace the resource at this exact URL.
- **PATCH**: apply a partial modification.
- **DELETE**: remove the resource.
- **OPTIONS**: ask what the server supports; used by CORS preflight.

Idempotency matters for retries: clients, proxies and libraries can safely retry an idempotent request after a timeout. For POST you need an idempotency key (for example an `Idempotency-Key` header) so the server can detect duplicates, which is how payment APIs avoid double charges.

lesson.heading: Status codes by class
lesson.body:
The first digit gives the class:

- **1xx informational**: `101 Switching Protocols` (WebSocket upgrade), `103 Early Hints`.
- **2xx success**: `200 OK`, `201 Created` (with a `Location` header for the new resource), `202 Accepted` (queued for async processing), `204 No Content`.
- **3xx redirection**: `301 Moved Permanently`, `302 Found`, `303 See Other`, `304 Not Modified` (cache revalidation), `307 Temporary Redirect`, `308 Permanent Redirect`.
- **4xx client error**: `400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized` (really "unauthenticated": no or invalid credentials), `403 Forbidden` (authenticated but not allowed), `404 Not Found`, `405 Method Not Allowed`, `409 Conflict`, `412 Precondition Failed`, `415 Unsupported Media Type`, `422 Unprocessable Content` (validation errors), `429 Too Many Requests` (rate limiting, often with `Retry-After`).
- **5xx server error**: `500 Internal Server Error`, `502 Bad Gateway` (proxy got a bad response from upstream), `503 Service Unavailable` (overloaded or in maintenance), `504 Gateway Timeout` (upstream did not answer in time).

The redirect detail interviewers like: 301 and 302 historically let clients change POST into GET on the follow-up request. 307 and 308 forbid changing the method and body. 303 explicitly says "go GET this other URL", which is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern after a form submit.

lesson.heading: Headers you should know
lesson.body:
Headers are case-insensitive name/value pairs (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send them lowercase).

Request headers:
- `Host`: the target host; required in HTTP/1.1 so one IP can serve many sites.
- `Accept`, `Accept-Encoding`, `Accept-Language`: content negotiation. The server picks a representation and should add `Vary` for caches.
- `Authorization`: credentials, for example `Bearer <token>` or `Basic <base64>`.
- `Cookie`: cookies the browser stored for this site.
- `Content-Type` and `Content-Length` for requests with a body.
- `If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since`: conditional requests for caching.
- `Origin` and `Referer`: where the request came from.

Response headers:
- `Content-Type` (for example `text/html; charset=utf-8`), `Content-Encoding` (`gzip`, `br`, `zstd`).
- `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Vary`.
- `Set-Cookie`, `Location` (redirect target or created resource).
- Security headers: `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

lesson.heading: Content negotiation and compression
lesson.body:
A single resource can have several representations: JSON or XML, English or French, gzip or Brotli. The client says what it accepts, the server picks one and labels it.

Compression is the most visible case. The browser sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd` and the server responds with `Content-Encoding: br` and a compressed body. Text formats (HTML, CSS, JS, JSON, SVG) typically shrink 70-90%. Do not compress already-compressed formats such as JPEG, PNG, WebP, video or zip files; it wastes CPU for no gain.

Because the response now depends on a request header, the server must send `Vary: Accept-Encoding` so that a shared cache does not hand a Brotli body to a client that cannot decode it.

keyPoints: HTTP is stateless; state comes from cookies, tokens or server-side sessions.
Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) do not change state; idempotent methods (safe ones plus PUT and DELETE) can be retried safely.
POST is neither safe nor idempotent; use idempotency keys when retries could duplicate work.
401 means not authenticated, 403 means authenticated but not allowed.
307 and 308 preserve the method and body; 303 tells the client to follow up with GET.
fetch() resolves on any HTTP status, including 404 and 500; check res.ok.
Send Vary when the response depends on a request header such as Accept-Encoding.

questions.prompt: Which method is idempotent but NOT safe?
questions.explanation: PUT changes server state (so it is not safe), but repeating the same PUT leaves the resource in the same state (so it is idempotent). GET and HEAD are both safe and idempotent; POST is neither.

questions.prompt: A logged-in user tries to open another customer's invoice and is not allowed. Which status fits best?
questions.explanation: The user is authenticated, so 401 is wrong; they lack permission for this resource, which is 403. Some APIs return 404 instead to avoid revealing that the resource exists.

questions.prompt: What is logged when the server responds with status 404?
questions.explanation: fetch only rejects for network errors (DNS failure, connection refused, CORS failure). A 404 is a successful HTTP exchange, so the promise resolves with `res.ok === false`.

questions.prompt: After a successful form POST, the server wants the browser to load the confirmation page with GET so a refresh does not resubmit. Which status should it use?
questions.explanation: 303 See Other explicitly tells the client to fetch the Location with GET. This is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern. 307 and 308 would repeat the POST.

questions.prompt: A reverse proxy forwards a request to an upstream app server that does not answer within the proxy timeout. What does the proxy usually return?
questions.explanation: 504 Gateway Timeout means a gateway or proxy did not get a timely response from upstream. 502 means it got an invalid response; 503 means the service is unavailable or overloaded.

questions.prompt: Which response header must a server send when it serves gzip to some clients and uncompressed bodies to others from the same URL?
questions.explanation: `Vary` tells caches which request headers were used to pick the representation, so they store separate variants and do not serve gzip to a client that did not ask for it.

questions.prompt: Because PUT is idempotent, sending the same PUT twice must return the same status code both times.
questions.explanation: Idempotency is about the effect on server state, not the response. The first PUT may return 201 Created and the second 200 OK or 204, while the resource ends up identical.

questions.prompt: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use the same methods, status codes and header semantics as HTTP/1.1.
questions.explanation: RFC 9110 defines HTTP semantics independently of the version. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 only change how messages are framed and transported.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which status codes indicate a client error?
questions.explanation: 4xx codes are client errors: 404 Not Found, 422 Unprocessable Content and 429 Too Many Requests. 502 is a server-side gateway error and 304 is a cache revalidation response.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the HTTP/1.1 request header that names the target domain so one IP can host many sites is ___.
questions.explanation: The Host header enables virtual hosting. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same information in the `:authority` pseudo-header.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between safe and idempotent methods, and why does it matter?
questions.answer:
- Safe means the client is not requesting any state change: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE. Caches, crawlers and link prefetchers rely on this, so a GET that deletes data is a real bug (a crawler can wipe your data).
- Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once: all safe methods plus PUT and DELETE.
- It matters for retries: browsers, HTTP clients, proxies and service meshes may automatically retry idempotent requests after a timeout or dropped connection.
- POST is neither, so a retried POST can create duplicate orders or charges. The standard fix is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and the server stores the result keyed by it, returning the stored result for duplicates.
- Note that idempotency refers to server state, not the response body or status code.

questions.prompt: Explain 401 vs 403, and 301 vs 302 vs 307 vs 308.
questions.answer:
- 401 Unauthorized: the request lacks valid authentication; the server should send WWW-Authenticate. The client can fix it by logging in or refreshing a token.
- 403 Forbidden: the server knows who you are and still refuses. Re-authenticating will not help. Some APIs return 404 to hide existence.
- 301 and 308 are permanent: clients and search engines should update links, and browsers cache them aggressively.
- 302 and 307 are temporary.
- The difference within each pair: 301 and 302 historically allowed changing POST into GET on redirect; 307 and 308 require keeping the same method and body. For API redirects of non-GET requests, use 307/308. 303 is the explicit "now GET this" used after form submissions.

questions.prompt: How would you design error responses for a JSON API?
questions.answer:
- Use the right status code class first, since clients, proxies and monitoring rely on it: 400 for malformed input, 401/403 for auth, 404, 409 for conflicts, 422 for validation failures, 429 with Retry-After for rate limits, 5xx only for server faults.
- Return a consistent machine-readable body. RFC 9457 Problem Details (application/problem+json) gives type, title, status, detail and instance, plus extension fields such as a list of field errors.
- Include a stable error code that clients can switch on, not just a human message that may change or be localized.
- Include a request or trace ID so support can find logs.
- Never leak stack traces, SQL or internal hostnames in production responses.

questions.prompt: Why does fetch() not reject on a 500 response, and how do you handle errors correctly?
questions.answer:
- fetch models the HTTP exchange: if a response arrived, the request succeeded at the network level, whatever the status. It rejects only for network failures, aborted requests (AbortController) and CORS blocks.
- So you must check res.ok (true for 200-299) or res.status and throw or branch yourself.
- A robust wrapper: set a timeout with AbortSignal.timeout(ms), check res.ok, parse the error body (problem+json) for a useful message, and retry only idempotent requests or requests with an idempotency key, with exponential backoff and jitter.
- Libraries like axios reject on non-2xx by default, which is one reason people find the behavior surprising when switching.

chapters.title: REST API Basics
chapters.summary: Designing resource-oriented HTTP APIs: URLs, methods, status codes, pagination, filtering and versioning.

lesson.heading: What REST actually means
lesson.body:
REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style described by Roy Fielding in 2000. Its constraints include client-server separation, **statelessness** (each request carries all needed context), **cacheability** (responses say whether they can be cached), a **uniform interface** (resources identified by URLs, manipulated through representations with standard methods), and a layered system (proxies and CDNs can sit in between).

In practice, "REST API" means a resource-oriented JSON-over-HTTP API that uses methods and status codes as intended. Few APIs implement full hypermedia (HATEOAS, where responses contain links that drive the next actions), and that is fine for most interviews, but you should know the term.

lesson.heading: Resources and URL design
lesson.body:
Model your API as **nouns** (resources) and let HTTP methods be the verbs.

- Collections are plural: `/users`, `/orders`.
- Items are addressed by ID: `/users/42`.
- Sub-resources express ownership: `/users/42/orders`.
- Avoid verbs in paths: `POST /orders`, not `POST /createOrder`. When an operation is not CRUD (cancel an order), either model it as a state change (`PATCH /orders/7` with `{"status":"cancelled"}`) or as a sub-resource action (`POST /orders/7/cancellation`).
- Use query parameters for filtering, sorting and pagination: `/orders?status=paid&sort=-createdAt&limit=20`.
- Keep URLs lowercase and use hyphens, and keep nesting shallow (two levels is usually enough).

code.source:
GET    /articles              # list (paginated)
POST   /articles              # create -> 201 Created + Location: /articles/123
GET    /articles/123          # read
PUT    /articles/123          # replace the whole article
PATCH  /articles/123          # partial update
DELETE /articles/123          # delete -> 204 No Content
GET    /articles/123/comments # sub-collection

lesson.heading: PUT vs PATCH vs POST
lesson.body:
- **POST /articles** creates a new article; the server assigns the ID and returns `201 Created` with a `Location` header. Repeating it creates another article.
- **PUT /articles/123** sends the complete representation. Fields you omit are reset or removed. It can also create the resource if the client chooses the ID. Idempotent.
- **PATCH /articles/123** sends only the changes. The common format is JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396, `application/merge-patch+json`) where `null` deletes a field; JSON Patch (RFC 6902) is a list of operations such as `{"op":"replace","path":"/title","value":"New"}`.

A common bug is implementing PUT as a partial update. Clients that rely on PUT semantics expect missing fields to be cleared.

lesson.heading: Pagination, filtering and consistency
lesson.body:
Never return unbounded collections.

- **Offset pagination** (`?limit=20&offset=40` or `?page=3`): simple and allows jumping to page N, but it gets slow on large offsets (the database still scans skipped rows) and items shift when rows are inserted or deleted between pages.
- **Cursor (keyset) pagination** (`?limit=20&after=eyJpZCI6MTIzfQ`): the cursor encodes the last seen sort key; the query becomes `WHERE id > 123 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`. It is fast at any depth and stable under inserts, but cannot jump to an arbitrary page. Feeds and large tables use it.

Return pagination metadata in the body (`nextCursor`, `hasMore`) or in a `Link` header. For concurrency control, return an `ETag` and require `If-Match` on updates; the server answers `412 Precondition Failed` if someone else changed the resource first, which prevents lost updates.

lesson.heading: Versioning, statelessness and REST vs alternatives
lesson.body:
**Versioning**: the most common approach is a version in the path (`/v1/orders`), because it is visible and easy to route. Alternatives are a header (`Api-Version: 2026-01-01`, which date-based APIs such as Stripe use) or media type versioning. Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields) so versions change rarely, and never remove or rename a field without a new version and a deprecation period.

**Statelessness**: the server should not rely on in-memory session state tied to one instance. Authentication travels with each request (a cookie referencing a shared session store, or a token). This lets any instance behind a load balancer handle any request and lets you scale horizontally.

**Alternatives**: GraphQL lets clients request exactly the fields they need in one round trip, which suits complex UIs, at the cost of harder HTTP caching and query cost control. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 for fast, typed service-to-service calls. REST remains the default for public APIs because it uses plain HTTP, caches well and every tool understands it.

keyPoints: REST models resources as nouns in URLs and uses HTTP methods as verbs.
POST creates with a server-chosen ID and returns 201 plus Location; PUT replaces fully; PATCH updates partially.
Statelessness lets any server instance handle any request, which enables horizontal scaling.
Cursor pagination is fast and stable on large or changing datasets; offset pagination allows page jumps but degrades.
ETag plus If-Match gives optimistic concurrency control and prevents lost updates (412 on conflict).
Prefer additive changes; version (path or header) only for breaking changes.

questions.prompt: Which endpoint best follows REST conventions for creating an order?
questions.explanation: The collection URL plus POST expresses creation. Verbs in the path duplicate what the method already says, and GET must never create data.

questions.prompt: A client sends `PUT /users/7` with `{"name":"Ann"}` and the stored user previously had name and email. Under correct PUT semantics, what happens to email?
options: It is removed or reset, because PUT replaces the whole resource
The server must reject the request with 400
questions.explanation: PUT means the body is the complete new state. For partial updates use PATCH. Many APIs implement PUT incorrectly as a merge, which surprises clients.

questions.prompt: What should a successful `POST /articles` return?
options: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new article
questions.explanation: 201 signals a new resource was created and Location gives its URL. Returning the created representation in the body is also common and saves a round trip.

questions.prompt: Your feed endpoint uses `?page=N` and users report duplicated items when scrolling while new posts arrive. What fixes this best?
options: Switch to cursor (keyset) pagination based on a stable sort key
Cache each page for an hour
questions.explanation: With offsets, new rows inserted at the top shift every later page, so items repeat. A cursor anchors on the last seen key, so inserts do not shift the window.

questions.prompt: Two users edit the same document. User B saves after user A, silently overwriting A's change. Which HTTP mechanism prevents this?
options: ETag with If-Match, returning 412 on mismatch
questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency: the client sends the ETag it read in If-Match; if the resource changed, the ETag differs and the server rejects with 412 Precondition Failed so the client can merge.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason REST APIs should be stateless?
options: Any server instance can handle any request, so you can scale and fail over freely
questions.explanation: When requests carry their own context (token or session ID resolved from a shared store), load balancers can route to any instance and instances can be added or removed.

questions.prompt: PATCH is guaranteed to be idempotent by the HTTP specification.
questions.explanation: PATCH is not defined as idempotent. A patch like 'increment counter' or a JSON Patch 'add to array' changes state on every call. It can be idempotent if designed that way (for example merge patch setting fixed values).

questions.prompt: Most production REST APIs fully implement HATEOAS (hypermedia links driving all client navigation).
questions.explanation: HATEOAS is part of Fielding's definition, but most real-world JSON APIs only use resource URLs, methods and status codes. Knowing the term is enough for most interviews.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are good practices for a public REST API?
options: Plural nouns for collections, such as `/orders`
Cursor pagination for large, frequently changing lists
Additive, backward-compatible changes instead of renaming fields
Using GET to trigger deletions so links work in emails
questions.explanation: Status codes should reflect errors so clients and monitoring work; GET must be safe. The other three are standard API design practice.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: after creating a resource, the server returns status 201 and the ___ header with the new resource URL.
questions.explanation: The Location header points to the newly created resource (and to the redirect target for 3xx responses).

questions.prompt: How would you design a REST API for a blog with posts and comments?
questions.answer:
- Resources: /posts, /posts/{id}, /posts/{id}/comments, /comments/{id} (top-level for direct edits so nesting stays shallow).
- Methods: GET list and item, POST to collections returning 201 + Location, PATCH for edits, DELETE returning 204.
- Listing: cursor pagination with limit, filters like ?author=12&tag=js, sort=-publishedAt; return nextCursor and hasMore.
- Validation errors as 422 with field-level problem details; 404 for missing posts; 403 when editing someone else's post.
- Caching: ETag on GET so clients get 304s; Cache-Control: public, max-age for published posts; If-Match on updates to prevent lost edits.
- Versioning: /v1 prefix or a version header; evolve additively.
- Auth via bearer token or session cookie, rate limiting with 429 and Retry-After.

questions.prompt: Compare offset and cursor pagination.
questions.answer:
- Offset (limit/offset or page numbers) is easy to implement and supports jumping to page N and showing total pages.
- But the database must still walk past skipped rows, so OFFSET 100000 is slow, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift results, causing duplicates or skipped items.
- Cursor (keyset) pagination remembers the last seen sort key (often an opaque base64 token encoding (createdAt, id)) and queries WHERE (createdAt, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY createdAt DESC, id DESC LIMIT n. With an index it is constant time at any depth and stable under writes.
- Downsides: no random page access, harder total counts, and the sort must be on a unique, indexed key (add id as a tiebreaker).
- Choose offset for small admin tables, cursor for feeds, infinite scroll and large datasets.

questions.prompt: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC: when would you choose each?
questions.answer:
- REST: the default for public and partner APIs. Plain HTTP, easy caching with CDNs and ETags, universal tooling, simple to reason about. Weakness: over-fetching or under-fetching, multiple round trips for nested data.
- GraphQL: one endpoint where clients ask for exactly the fields they need; strong typed schema and great for complex UIs aggregating many backends. Costs: HTTP caching is harder (mostly POST, one URL), you need query depth/cost limits, N+1 resolver problems need batching (DataLoader), and error handling is nonstandard (200 with errors array).
- gRPC: Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, contract-first, fast binary encoding, streaming in both directions, generated clients. Great for internal service-to-service calls; poor fit for browsers without a proxy (gRPC-Web).
- Many systems combine them: gRPC internally, REST or GraphQL at the edge.

questions.prompt: How do you evolve an API without breaking existing clients?
questions.answer:
- Make changes additive: new optional fields, new endpoints, new enum values documented as possible. Clients should ignore unknown fields.
- Never remove, rename or change the type or meaning of a field in place.
- For breaking changes, introduce a new version (/v2 or a dated version header), run both, announce deprecation with timelines, and signal it with the Deprecation and Sunset headers.
- Track usage per version and per client to know when you can turn off the old one.
- Use contract tests or schema diffing (OpenAPI) in CI to catch accidental breaking changes.
